claims.claim: Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213–c. 270); Origen's pupil; apostle of Pontus.
Annunciation homilies transmitted under his name but generally counted spurious/later.
SCOPE: the whole First Discourse (Homily I); Homilies II and III are not translated.
Gregory Thaumaturgus was a Christian bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus (modern Niksar, Turkey) who lived from approximately 213 to 270 AD.
He was originally named Theodore and was born to a pagan family, converting to Christianity after studying with Origen at Caesarea in Palestine.
He was ordained bishop of Neocaesarea by Phaedimus of Amasea, reportedly while Gregory was in hiding in the wilderness.
The work consists of four homilies, three of which are on the Annunciation and one on the Baptism of Our Lord.
The homilies on the Annunciation were delivered as festival sermons celebrating the mystery of the Annunciation to the Virgin Mary.
The homilies address the mystery of the Incarnation, including Mary's virginity, the role of the Holy Spirit, and the fulfillment of prophecy.
The work survives in manuscript tradition and has been transmitted among the writings of Gregory Thaumaturgus, though its authenticity has been disputed by some scholars.
The homily has been cited to prove the antiquity of the festival of the Annunciation observed on March 25 in the West.
Gregory Thaumaturgus was a champion of orthodoxy in the 3rd-century Trinitarian controversy and participated in the Council of Antioch (c. 264) that condemned Paul of Samosata.
His surviving theological writings have reached us in a very incomplete state, which partially obscures his historical importance despite his well-authenticated life.
